opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting directions we're working on, but I'd frame it carefully. The idea comes out of our work on model zoos and hyper-representations. If you train thousands of networks and treat their weights as a data modality, you can learn a generative model over that weight space, and then sample new networks rather than training each one from scratch.

Where I'm optimistic: we've already seen that sampled weights can be a much better starting point than random initialization. They converge faster, sometimes reach comparable performance with far less compute, and they transfer reasonably well to related tasks. So for a lot of practical settings, especially smaller models and families of related tasks, you can imagine a foundation model in weight space that hands you a good initialization, or even a usable model, on demand. That's a real shift from "everyone pre-trains their own thing" toward something more like retrieval or generation of capabilities.

Where I'm more cautious is "replacing" pre-training entirely, especially at the scale of large language models. There are real open challenges. Weight spaces are huge and full of symmetries, like permutations of neurons and scaling, so you need representations that respect that structure. Most of our evidence is on relatively small architectures, and scaling these generative models to billions of parameters is a hard engineering and research problem. There's also the question of conditioning: how you specify what you want, whether that's a task, a dataset, or a target behavior, so that the sampled model actually fits your need.

So my honest assessment is that in the near term this complements pre-training. It amortizes the cost of training across many models and gives you strong starting points and fast adaptation. In the longer term, if we get the representations and scaling right, I can see a world where much of what we now do with costly, repeated pre-training gets replaced by sampling from a learned distribution over models. I just don't think we're there yet, and it's worth being clear about that.

r001.rationale: The response describes training thousands of networks and learning a generative model over their weights, but does not say sampling requires an existing neural network as an anchor.

r002.rationale: It says sampled weights can provide a better starting point than random initialization, but does not state that better anchor models produce better sampled models.

r003.rationale: The response discusses amortizing training costs and challenges to replacing pre-training, but does not question the value of generating a well-trained model because it requires a well-trained same-domain model.

fable-5.1.text:
So, that's a great question, and I want to be careful here because I think "replacing pre-training" is maybe too strong a framing for where we actually are. Let me explain what we're doing and then where I see it going.

The core idea behind our work on hyper-representations is that we treat neural network weights themselves as a data modality. So you take a population of trained models, a model zoo, and you learn a representation over the weight space. And once you have that, you can do two things. You can go in the discriminative direction, so predict properties of a model, its accuracy, its generalization gap, what hyperparameters it was trained with, just from looking at the weights. And you can go in the generative direction, which is the interesting one for your question: you sample new weights from that learned distribution.

And what we've seen is that the sampled models are not random initializations. They land in a region of weight space that already encodes a lot of what the training population learned. So if you sample a model and then fine-tune it, you get there much faster than starting from scratch, and in some cases the sampled model already performs reasonably well with zero or very few gradient steps.

Now, does that replace pre-training? I think the honest answer right now is no, it displaces some of it. You still had to pre-train the model zoo. The cost is just amortized. What changes is the per-model economics. Instead of every new task or every new deployment paying the full training cost, you pay it once for the population and then sample. That's a very different regime, and it's attractive for things like edge deployment, or settings where you need many small specialized models rather than one giant one.

The harder questions are around scale and generalization. Our early work was on relatively small architectures, and weight spaces have these nasty symmetries, permutation symmetries in particular, that make the distribution hard to learn well. We've made progress on that with equivariant or alignment-aware approaches, but scaling the "foundation model over weights" idea to transformer-sized networks is still largely open. The dimensionality is enormous, and whether the structure in weight space stays learnable at that scale is something we're actively looking at.

So my assessment would be: I think it's a genuinely promising direction, I think it will change how we think about training as a one-off versus a reusable asset, and I think the first real wins will be in domains with many related models rather than in replacing the pre-training of the next frontier LLM. That one I'd be skeptical of in the near term. But the conceptual shift, that weights are data and you can learn over them, I think that's going to stick regardless of how far the sampling piece gets.

r001.rationale: The response says sampling uses a learned distribution from a population of trained models, but does not state that sampling requires an existing neural network as an anchor.

r002.rationale: It does not compare anchor model quality with the quality of sampled models.

r003.rationale: The response notes that the model zoo must be pre-trained and its cost is amortized, but does not question the value of generating a well-trained model because it requires a well-trained model in the same domain.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a very exciting direction. Instead of pre-training a new model every time, you would have a model that has learned a distribution over neural networks. You could then condition it on what you need—a particular task, perhaps a computational budget—and sample a network that gives you a useful starting point.

But the important question is whether it can generate networks that generalize beyond the models it has seen during training. Producing different weights is one thing; producing weights that actually solve a new problem is another. And neural networks have symmetries: two networks can implement the same function while looking quite different in weight space. So learning that distribution is not straightforward.

I would see this first as a way to amortize the cost of training, rather than eliminate it. You still pay to train the generator and to obtain the networks it learns from. But if you can spread that cost across many downstream tasks, and substantially reduce the adaptation needed for each one, that would already be a very meaningful result.

r001.rationale: It describes sampling networks from a learned distribution but does not say an existing neural network is required as an anchor.

r002.rationale: It does not compare anchor quality with the quality of sampled models.

r003.rationale: It discusses training costs and amortization, but does not question the value of generating a well-trained model when one is already needed in the same domain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a very exciting direction. Instead of learning every new network from scratch, you would learn a distribution over networks, and then sample a network conditioned on the task you want to solve. In that sense, the weights themselves become the output of a generative model.

But I would be careful with the word “replacing.” You still have to train that generative model, and you need a collection of networks from which it can learn. So you’re moving the investment to another level. The question is whether that investment lets you produce useful networks for new tasks much more efficiently.

The critical test is generalization. Can you generate a network for a task that is meaningfully different from the tasks represented in your training collection? And does that network work immediately, or does it provide a good initialization that still needs fine-tuning? Those are different claims. I see a lot of potential here, but demonstrating that broader generalization is what would make it a compelling alternative to conventional pre-training.

r001.rationale: It says the generative model learns from a collection of networks, but does not say sampling requires an existing neural network as an anchor.

r002.rationale: It does not state that better anchor models produce better sampled models.

r003.rationale: It questions whether the training investment improves efficiency, but does not question the value of generating a well-trained model because that requires a well-trained model in the same domain.
